title: Gonja: The Kingdom of the Horsemen

pages.text: In the village of Larabanga, near Mole National Park, stands a small mosque unlike any modern building. Its walls are made of mud, painted white, and held up by thick buttresses. Dark wooden poles stick out from the towers like the quills of a porcupine. The same style can be seen far away in Mali, along the River Niger. Nobody is sure of the mosque’s age, but it is among the oldest in Ghana. It is a sign that people, ideas, and faith once travelled here from the north-west. Those travellers built the kingdom of Gonja.

pages.text: About five hundred years ago, the great empire of Mali controlled much of the gold trade of West Africa. Tradition says that a party of Mande horsemen rode south-east from Mali towards the lands where the gold came from. With them came Muslim scholars and traders. They did not go home. They settled among the peoples north of the Black Volta. They married local women and in time spoke the local language. From this meeting of newcomers and older inhabitants, a new ruling group arose. They were known as the Ngbanya, and their state was Gonja.

pages.alt: A group of horsemen in robes and turbans riding through tall grass beside a broad river.

pages.text: The hero of Gonja history is Ndewura Jakpa, who lived in the 1600s. His name is said to mean the lord who conquers with the spear. Riding at the head of his horsemen, Jakpa pushed the borders of Gonja east and south until the kingdom stretched across much of the savanna of what is now northern Ghana. He is said to have had Muslim advisers who prayed for his victories. When he grew old, he divided the land among his sons. Each became chief of a division, such as Bole, Wasipe, Kpembe, Tuluwe, and Kusawgu.

pages.text: This sharing shaped the way Gonja is governed. The king of all Gonja is called the Yagbonwura. He does not come from one royal house only. The kingship rotates: it passes in turn among the leading divisions founded by Jakpa’s sons. So every division knows that its turn will come, and none is shut out for ever. The Yagbonwura’s seat is at Damongo. Gonja has another treasure. In the 1700s, its Muslim scholars wrote down the history of the kingdom in Arabic. This chronicle is one of the oldest written histories made in Ghana.

pages.text: Gonja’s wealth came from standing in the middle. In the forest to the south grew kola nuts, which do not grow in the dry north. Asante traders carried kola to the Gonja town of Salaga. There they met caravans from Hausaland, Mossi country, and beyond, bringing cloth, leather, salt, horses, and cattle. For a time, Salaga was one of the busiest markets in West Africa. It had a dark side as well. Captives were sold there as slaves, and the old wells and market ground are kept today as a place of memory. In the 1700s, Asante made Gonja pay tribute.

pages.text: What does Gonja leave us? First, it shows that Ghana’s history has never stopped at its borders. Horsemen from Mali, scholars writing Arabic, and caravans from Hausaland all helped to make a Ghanaian kingdom. Second, it shows one way of sharing power, by letting it rotate so that every division has a turn. Third, at Salaga, it teaches us to remember the painful parts of the past as honestly as the proud ones. Each year, the people of Damongo and other Gonja towns celebrate the Damba festival, and the drums praise Jakpa’s name once more.

activities.question: According to tradition, where did the founders of Gonja come from?
How is the Yagbonwura chosen?
options: The kingship rotates among the leading divisions
By an election of all citizens
He is always the eldest son of the last king

activities.question: Why did Salaga become a great market?
options: Kola from the forest met caravans from the north there

activities.question: Apply it: Three houses in a school each want their own member to be sports captain every year. Which Gonja idea could solve the quarrel?
options: Let the biggest house always win
Rotate the position so that each house has its turn
